results.content: Reviewed by: Xavier Jouve, Ph.D. Measurement invariance is the statistical property ensuring that a test measures the same construct across different groups, times, or conditions. Measurement invariance, also known as measurement equivalence, is a fundamental psychometric property that determines whether a test measures the same construct in the same way across different groups, occasions, or conditions. * Learn methods for testing invariance using confirmatory factor analysis. The most common approach to testing measurement invariance involves multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA). Invariance testing is fundamental to ensuring test fairness across demographic groups. Violations of measurement invariance indicate potential test bias, where individuals from different groups with equal ability levels receive different scores. Effect sizes for non-invariance, such as dMACS for mean differences or R-square changes, provide practical significance beyond statistical tests. Recent methodological advances include approximate measurement invariance using Bayesian methods, alignment optimization for many groups, and moderated nonlinear factor analysis for continuous moderators. Measurement invariance testing is essential for ethical test use but requires expertise in psychometric methods.

Among them are (1) the number and order of tests required to establish measurement invariance, (2) the criteria used to evaluate model fit, (3) partial invariance, and (4) the sample and model characteristics that may moderate invariance. Here, we document the levels of invariance (no, partial, full) achieved for each invariance step tested (configural, metric, scalar, residual) in a sampling of articles published over a 1-year period, and explore whether model fit criteria, sample size, number of groups being compared, and model size (as indexed by model degrees of freedom) relate to the invariance level (no, partial, full) achieved for each step. This study examined the measurement invariance of responses to the patient-reported outcomes measurement information system (PROMIS) pain behavior (PB) item bank in two samples: the PROMIS calibration sample (Wave 1, _N_ = 426) and a sample recruited from the American Chronic Pain Association (ACPA, _N_ = 750). ### Methods Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA) and two item response theory (IRT)-based differential item functioning (DIF) approaches were employed to evaluate the existence of measurement invariance. Demographics between the PROMIS Wave 1 sample and the ACPA sample for pain behavior Open in a new tab _PROMIS_ patient-reported outcomes measurement information system, _ACPA_ American Chronic Pain Association ### MG-CFA approach #### Configural invariance A configural invariance model (i.e., the same pattern of item-factor loadings across groups) was tested across the comparison groups. Results of testing measurement invariance of the pain behavior items across PROMIS Wave 1 and ACPA using MG-CFA Open in a new tab Measurement invariance tests included 27 items after deleing PB2, PB9, PB16, PB23, PB24, PB29, PB31, PB43, and PB53 items from the initial 36 items _CFI_ comparative fit index, _TLI_ Tucker–Lewis index, _RMSEA_ root mean square error of approximation, _CI_ confidence interval, n.a. not applicable #### Metric invariance A metric invariance model (i.e., equal constraints on unstandardized item-factor loadings across groups) also supported good fit: χ 2 (675, _N_ = 1,176) = 3,486.512, _p_< .01, CFI = 0.904, TLI = 0.900, RMSEA = 0.084 (from 0.081 to 0.087). The current study examined the measurement invariance of PB items using MG-CFA across two samples to evaluate whether the construct of PBs is the same in healthy people and those with chronic pain.
